scope: Appendix D.2.b, Eqs. (D2)–(D4). Each one-qubit Pauli tensor its own copy is diagonal in the Bell basis. The identity reconstructs its matrix entries by summing Bell projectors times their measured signs, including the sign for Y⊗Y.
The algebra underlying Appendix D.2.b, Eq. (D6), extends to any complex matrix ρ. Contracting the Bell readouts against ρ⊗ρ gives Tr(ρP)². This extension uses a complex square.

Appendix D.2.b, Eq. (D6). For Hermitian ρ and any Pauli word P, the product of local Bell signs on two copies has Born-weighted sum |Tr(ρP)|². For a density operator this is the expectation under the Bell measurement. The measurement is independent of P.
For each local X, Y or Z measurement, adding its two eigenprojectors gives the identity. Weighting them by their signs recovers the measured Pauli operator.
For a fixed choice of local axes and an arbitrary matrix on the k-qubit support, finite summation factors a product statistic over outcomes into local signed-projector sums inside the Born trace.

For a weight-k Pauli string on its support, the single-shot local Pauli shadow equals zero unless all k axes match. Multiplying the matched outcome sign by 3ᵏ gives Born mean Tr(ρP). The trace identity extends linearly to arbitrary complex matrices.

Supplementary Lemma 3, Eq. (S50). For every trace-one matrix on the k-qubit support, the single-shot Pauli estimator has second moment exactly 3ᵏ. On reduced density matrices this is the state-independent moment underlying the paper’s squared shadow norm.
The single-shot Pauli readout is real because it is a real scale times a product of measured signs. This relates its real-valued random variable to the Born trace identities.

For N independent uniformly chosen local Pauli shots with the Born marginal on a weight-k support, Chebyshev’s inequality gives probability at most 3ᵏ/(Nε²) that the block mean misses its target by ε or more. The proof uses unbiasedness and the exact second moment in Supplementary Lemma 3.
The median is the middle order statistic. If an odd sample of 2r+1 values has median error at least ε, at least r+1 distinct values also have error at least ε.
With mutually independent block estimates, each failing with probability at most 1/8, a union bound over subsets of r+1 bad blocks bounds the median’s failure probability by 1/(4·2ʳ).

Supplementary Theorem 1 for finite families of Pauli words and uniform local Pauli measurements. Reusing N shots per block across M targets of possibly different supports, Nε²≥8·3ᵏ for every target of weight k gives simultaneous failure probability at most M/(4·2ʳ) with 2r+1 independent blocks.

Supplementary Theorem 1 specialized to local Pauli shadows, with a different explicit constant choice. For δ,ε>0 use 2r+1 blocks where r is the ceiling binary logarithm of ⌈M/(4δ)⌉. The Pauli Born marginals, independent draws and Nε²≥8·3ᵏ on each target imply simultaneous failure probability at most δ.

For a bijective finite unitary-basis measurement channel in positive finite dimension and any Hermitian A, the squared shadow norm of Eq. (S7) is attained as the largest Born-record second moment over density states. Qatlib proves this through the positive moment effect.

Supplementary Theorem 1 for arbitrary finite families of Hermitian observables and finite, invertible unitary-basis measurement ensembles. Qatlib constructs the Born record law and inverse snapshots. With K independent blocks of L shared shots and Lε² at least four times every centered squared shadow norm, the simultaneous failure probability is at most M·3^⌊K/2⌋/2ᴷ.
The finite unitary ensemble version of Eq. (S7). In positive dimension, the positive moment effect attains the maximal second moment over density operators for any Hermitian observable.

Supplementary Theorem 1 for arbitrary Hermitian observables and finite unitary ensembles. The independent Born samples and inverse snapshots are explicit. A per-observable centered squared shadow norm at most Lε²/4 yields simultaneous failure probability at most M·3^⌊K/2⌋/2ᴷ.
